# What this document is

You are being handed a set of **HLA genotypes** for `r f("n_typed")` people —
`r f("n_typed_PH")` CTEPH cases and `r f("n_typed_AGP3K")` AGP3K controls — so that you
can test whether any of them associates with disease. **CTEPH** is chronic
thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension, the disease under study; **AGP3K** is the
Japanese cohort the controls are drawn from.

This document has one job: to let you use those genotypes **without having to trust them
blindly**. It says what was measured, how completely, how well it agrees with published
data, and — most importantly — the two specific ways it can mislead you if you are not
careful. @sec-completeness through @sec-confound are the quality evidence;
@sec-support is the part to read before you design an analysis.

# HLA in five minutes {#sec-primer}

Skip this section if you already know what `A*24:02` means. Everything after it assumes
you have read it — the gene names, the notation, the two different ways a call can be
missing, and why DRB3 keeps coming back.

## Where these genes are

The **HLA** genes (Human Leukocyte Antigen) are not scattered around the genome. They sit
together on the short arm of chromosome 6, at band 6p21.3, inside a region called the
**MHC** (Major Histocompatibility Complex): roughly three to four megabases, and one of
the most gene-dense stretches of the human genome. MHC is the generic name for that region
in any species; HLA is what the human copy of it is called.

The region is conventionally read in three blocks along the chromosome. Starting from the
centromeric end: the **class II** genes (DP, DM, DO, DQ, DR), then a **class III** block
that contains no HLA genes at all but is packed with other immune genes — complement,
TNF — and then the **class I** genes, B and C, then E, then A, with the non-classical G
and F furthest towards the telomere. Class III matters here only because it sits between
the other two and is inherited with them.

This delivery types `r f("n_genes_typed")` genes from that region and turns
`r f("n_genes_with_residues")` of them into amino-acid residues. The difference is not a
quality filter: the rest are pseudogenes — DRB2, DRB6–DRB9, DPA2 and the class I
pseudogenes H, J, K, L, T, V, W and Y — and IPD-IMGT publishes no protein alignment for a
gene that makes no protein.

### You have two copies of chromosome 6, and that is the unit everything is counted in

One copy came from each parent, so you carry **two copies of every gene in this region**,
and the two copies can carry different alleles — that is what it means to be heterozygous.

From @sec-completeness onward, every count in this document is per **chromosome copy**, not
per person. The `r f("n_typed_AGP3K")` controls therefore contribute twice that many copies
at a locus where everyone was typed. So a figure of a few thousand "control chromosomes" is
not a few thousand different chromosomes: it is this cohort, counted twice over. Frequencies
have to be counted that way, because a person carries an allele zero, one or two times and
counting heads would throw that distinction away.

It also explains a number that otherwise looks broken. DRB3, DRB4 and DRB5 are missing
outright from many copies (below), so their denominator is not the full count — DRB3 is
called on `r f("frac_chr_ctrl_not_comparable_jmorp")` of control chromosomes, and only the
copies that actually carry the gene are counted. That difference is the whole of @sec-drb3.

## Class I and class II do the same job on different threats

An HLA protein holds a short fragment of another protein — a **peptide** — in a groove on
its outer surface and displays it, so that passing T cells can inspect what the cell is
carrying. That is the whole function. The two classes differ in where the peptide came
from, which cells do the displaying, and who is watching.

| | class I | class II |
|---|---|---|
| classical genes | HLA-A, -B, -C | HLA-DR, -DQ, -DP |
| how the molecule is built | one variable α chain, plus β2-microglobulin, an invariant partner encoded outside the MHC entirely | two chains, both encoded here: DRA + DRB1/3/4/5, DQA1 + DQB1, DPA1 + DPB1 |
| displayed by | every nucleated cell | antigen-presenting cells — dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells, thymic epithelium |
| peptide source | proteins made *inside* the cell: its own, a virus's, a tumour's | proteins taken in from *outside* and broken up in endosomes |
| peptide shape | short, groove closed at both ends | longer, groove open at both ends |
| inspected by | CD8 T cells | CD4 T cells |
| what a recognised peptide triggers | kill this cell | help — antibody production, cytokines, T-cell help |

Four of the genes typed here are class II but present nothing: **DMA, DMB, DOA and DOB**
encode the machinery that loads and edits peptides onto the class II molecules rather than
the molecules themselves. They are nearly invariant, which is why they contribute almost
no testable positions in @fig-qc (d). The same is true of **DRA**: the DR α chain barely
varies, so essentially all DR variation lives on the β chain — DRB1, and the DRB3/4/5
genes below.

The class I genes **HLA-E, -F and -G** are called *non-classical*. They are far less
variable than A, B and C and do specialised work — E reports on the health of the classical
class I supply to natural killer cells, G is expressed at the maternal–foetal interface.
They are typed here and they are informative about typing quality, but they are not where
a classical disease association is expected to be.

## Why this is the most variable region in the genome

Which peptides an HLA molecule can hold is decided by the shape of its groove, and the
groove is built from a handful of amino acids that line it. A population in which everyone
carried the same groove could be emptied by a single pathogen whose peptides that groove
cannot hold. Selection therefore rewards **being different from your neighbour**, and the
result is a locus with tens of thousands of known versions, where the common ones are held
at appreciable frequency for a very long time instead of drifting away.

Two things follow that matter for the rest of this document. The variation is
**concentrated**: it clusters in the exons that build the groove, and the rest of each gene
is comparatively quiet. And because the variation changes what the immune system can see,
HLA is associated with more diseases than any other region of the genome — autoimmunity,
infection, transplant rejection, drug hypersensitivity. If a disease has an immune
component, HLA is worth testing.

## The MHC is inherited in blocks

Recombination is suppressed across much of the MHC, so alleles at neighbouring genes are
not inherited independently. They travel as **haplotypes** — fixed combinations that recur
in a population far more often than chance would give — and the statistical shadow of that
is **linkage disequilibrium**: knowing someone's HLA-B allele tells you a great deal about
their HLA-C and often about their DRB1. Some of these blocks are megabases long and
population-specific; the Japanese haplotype carrying `A*24:02`, `C*12:02`, `B*52:01`,
`DRB1*15:02` and `DQB1*06:01` together is a well-known example.

::: {.callout-note}
## What this costs you when you interpret a result

An HLA association is a statement about a **block**, not about a gene, until you do extra
work to say otherwise. A signal at DQB1 may be carried by the DRB1 allele beside it, or by
a class III gene between them. Two consequences are practical: **you cannot localise a hit
to one gene from association statistics alone**, and the `r f("n_residue_columns")` residue
columns in this delivery are nowhere near `r f("n_residue_columns")` independent tests.
Conditional analysis — refitting with the strongest signal held fixed — is the usual next
step, and it is honest about how rarely it separates neighbours cleanly.
:::

## Typing is a matching problem, not a base call

For an ordinary variant you read one position and report one of two letters. HLA does not
work that way. The genes are so variable that the useful question is not "which letter is
at this position" but **"which of the thousands of known versions of this gene is this?"**
— and you have two of them, one from each parent.

So typing is a *matching* problem. Take the reads from the HLA region, compare them against
a catalogue of every version anyone has ever deposited, and decide which pair of catalogue
entries explains the reads best. The catalogue is **IPD-IMGT/HLA**, the international
registry that both names alleles and publishes their sequences; this run used release
`r f("imgt_release")`, held as a fixed copy on our own disk. That pinning matters: the
public catalogue is revised several times a year, alleles gain fields and occasionally get
renamed, and a reference that moves under a study is not a reference.

One property of matching is worth stating plainly, because @sec-confound turns on it:
**a version that is not in the catalogue cannot be returned.** A genuinely novel allele is
never reported as novel; its reads are assigned to the closest catalogued neighbour.

## What "a call" is here, and why short reads make it hard

A **call** is the pair of catalogue alleles that best explains one person's reads at one
gene, produced by HLA-HD `r f("hlahd_version")`. It is not a base call and it carries no
per-call probability. Three things make that hard to get right from short-read
whole-genome sequencing.

The differences that separate two alleles are spread along the gene, usually further apart
than a single read or read pair spans, so which difference sits on which chromosome has to
be inferred rather than seen. The reference genome carries **one arbitrary version** of
each HLA gene, so reads from a divergent allele mismatch it badly and map somewhere else or
nowhere at all — which is why the reads behind this delivery were pulled from every
alternate and HLA-specific contig in the reference as well as from chromosome 6 itself. And
the genes resemble one another: DRB1 and DRB3/4/5 are close paralogues, as are A, B and C
and the class I pseudogenes beside them, so reads from one gene are readily attracted to
another.

When several catalogue pairs fit the reads equally well the program says so, and this
dataset carries `r f("n_ambiguous_gene_calls")` such **ambiguous** results out of
`r f("n_gene_calls")` (sample, gene) calls. That flag is the closest thing to a confidence
score the method offers. **`failed` is the label that would mean something went wrong, and
it occurs `r f("n_failed_gene_calls")` times here.**

## How to read an allele name

A version of an HLA gene is called an **allele**, and its name is a structured address, not
an arbitrary label:

```
A * 24 : 02 : 01 : 03
│   │    │    │    └── field 4: a difference outside the protein-coding part
│   │    │    └─────── field 3: a DNA difference that does NOT change the protein
│   │    └──────────── field 2: a difference that DOES change the protein
│   └───────────────── field 1: the allele group, roughly the old serological type
└───────────────────── the gene, also called the locus

A * 24 : 09 N
            └── expression suffix: this allele is transcribed but no protein
                reaches the cell surface, so this chromosome presents nothing
                at HLA-A — even though its name looks like an ordinary A*24
```

The fields run from most consequential to least, and every allele has at least the first
two. The optional trailing letter is an **expression suffix**, and it overrides everything
to its left:

| suffix | means | why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| `N` | **null** — no protein on the cell surface | that chromosome is functionally empty at that gene, however normal the rest of the name looks |
| `L` | low surface expression | present, but at a level that may not behave like a full copy |
| `S` | secreted — the protein exists but is soluble, not on the membrane | the same caveat, for a different reason |
| `Q` | expression questionable, not yet established | treat as unresolved rather than as either of the above |

`N` is the one to remember. It is the mechanism behind the DRB4 discussion in
@sec-harmonise, where the reference panel uses a null allele to mean "this haplotype has no
working DRB4". Note also that **the names in this delivery never carry a suffix** — our
caller does not write them (@sec-harmonise) — so nothing in `allele_dosage.tsv` announces
itself as null.

## Why this delivery stops at two fields

**Field 2 is where the protein changes**, so it is the last field that changes what the
molecule can display. Everything beyond it is either silent at the protein level (field 3)
or outside the coding sequence entirely (field 4). This delivery therefore reports
`A*24:02` and stops.

That is a choice, but not much of one. Deeper fields are read from intronic and
untranslated sequence that short-read data covers unevenly, so they are the least reliable
part of a call: the deepest resolution reached anywhere in this dataset is field
`r f("max_field_depth_seen")`, and `r f("n_field4_calls")` calls carry a fourth. Published
population data is written at two fields as well, so a deeper delivery could not have been
compared against anything.

## The antigen recognition domain

Not all of an HLA protein is doing the presenting. The part that forms the groove and
contacts the peptide is the **antigen recognition domain** (ARD): the α1 and α2 segments
for class I, the α1 or β1 segment for class II — in DNA terms, exons 2 and 3 for a class I
gene and exon 2 for a class II gene.

The ARD is the natural unit for asking whether two alleles are functionally the same, and
IPD-IMGT uses it exactly that way: alleles whose protein is identical **across the ARD**
are collected into a **P group**, named after the lowest-numbered member with a `P`
appended. `DRB3*01:01P` is not an allele; it is a group of alleles that differ only outside
the groove. Reference panels frequently publish at that resolution, which is what
@sec-harmonise is about. The genotypes you were given are not P-grouped.

## Residues, and why they are often the better test

A **residue** is one amino acid at one position in the protein. Because a
`GENE:position:aminoacid` combination is shared by many different alleles, a residue test
asks a more robust question than an allele test:

| | allele test | residue test |
|---|---|---|
| what you regress on | one column of `allele_dosage.tsv`, e.g. `DRB1*15:01` | one column of `residue_dosage.tsv`, e.g. `DRB1:11:P` |
| the question it asks | "do people carrying `DRB1*15:01` get the disease more?" | "do people with a proline at DRB1 position 11 get it more?" |
| number of things tested | many, most of them rare | fewer, most of them common |
| if one rare allele is mis-called | that allele's result is wrong | usually unchanged — the allele it was confused with carries the same amino acid at most positions |
| what it cannot do | — | name the allele responsible; a residue is shared across many |

Concretely: this cohort carries `r f("n_alleles_carried")` distinct two-field alleles, and
the protein variation underneath them reduces to `r f("n_polymorphic_positions")` varying
amino-acid positions. The same evidence, in fewer and commoner columns.

Positions are numbered as IPD-IMGT numbers them, on the mature protein, which is why you
will see negative positions such as `A:-21:M` — those lie in the signal peptide that is cut
off during processing. Both matrices are delivered; @sec-support says which to trust when
they disagree.

## Genes you may not have: DRB3, DRB4 and DRB5

Most genes come in two copies. The DR region does not work that way. Every haplotype
carries DRA and DRB1, but whether it carries a *second* expressed β chain gene — and which
one — depends on the DRB1 allele it carries. The haplotype groups have names of their own:

| haplotype group | second β gene | carried with DRB1 groups |
|---|---|---|
| DR51 | DRB5 | `DRB1*15`, `DRB1*16` |
| DR52 | DRB3 | `DRB1*03`, `*11`, `*12`, `*13`, `*14` |
| DR53 | DRB4 | `DRB1*04`, `*07`, `*09` |
| — | none | `DRB1*01`, `*08`, `*10` |

So a person can genuinely carry **two copies, one copy, or none** of DRB3, DRB4 or DRB5,
and the fraction of this cohort in whom each gene was found at all reflects exactly that:
`r f("call_rate_DRB3")` for DRB3, `r f("call_rate_DRB4")` for DRB4 and
`r f("call_rate_DRB5")` for DRB5. That is biology, not a sequencing failure, and it
produces two of the outcome labels you will see in @sec-completeness:

* **hemizygous** — one copy present, one genuinely absent.
* **not typed** — the gene is absent from that person's haplotype altogether.

Neither means anything went wrong. It does mean that the dosage columns for these three
genes cannot be read like the others, that the reference comparison at DRB3 breaks down
(@sec-drb3), and that these are the genes @sec-support tells you not to use.

# What you are getting

Four tables, all keyed on `sample_id`, all covering exactly the same
**`r f("n_typed")`** people.

| file | shape | one column is | one cell is |
|---|---|---|---|
| `04.residues/allele_dosage.tsv` | `r f("n_typed")` × `r f("n_allele_columns")` | one 2-field allele, e.g. `A*24:02` | how many copies (0, 1, 2) |
| `04.residues/residue_dosage.tsv` | `r f("n_typed")` × `r f("n_residue_columns")` | one `GENE:position:aminoacid` | how many copies (0, 1, 2) |
| `04.residues/residue_diplotype.tsv` | `r f("n_typed")` × `r f("n_diplotype_columns")` | one `GENE:position` | the unordered pair of amino acids |
| `05.qc/allele_pgroup_map.tsv` | one row per allele | — | whether a published Japanese panel lists this allele at all |

The first two are what you will regress on. The fourth is the safety check
@sec-confound tells you to apply before testing a rare allele.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Read `sample_id` as a string, always

`r f("n_leading_zero_ids")` of the `r f("n_typed")` sample ids begin with a zero.
`pandas.read_csv` without `dtype` turns the column into an integer and silently deletes
those zeros; an inner join then returns `r f("n_after_numeric_join")` rows instead of
`r f("n_typed")`, with no error and no warning.

```python
pd.read_csv(path, sep='\t', dtype={'sample_id': str})
```
:::

# Which people these cover {#sec-people}

Three filters were applied in order, and **they are not the same kind of decision**.

```{r chain}
#| echo: true
data.frame(
  step = c("1. in the v6 study cohort", "2. passed sequencing quality control",
           "3. **in the mainland ancestry cluster**"),
  `what it selects for` = c("being part of this study at all",
                            "the genome-wide data being usable",
                            "**sharing an ancestry background**"),
  remaining = c(f("n_v6_flagged"), f("n_qc_pass"), f("n_typed")),
  removed = c("—", f("n_dropped_sample_qc"), f("n_dropped_ancestry")),
  check.names = FALSE
) |> kable()
```

Step 2 is a **quality** decision: `r f("n_dropped_sample_qc")` people whose genome-wide
heterozygosity was anomalous were dropped upstream. For HLA typing those are exactly the
samples least likely to resolve cleanly into two versions of a gene, so inheriting that
decision is the right thing to do.

Step 3 is an **ancestry** decision, and it is the one worth understanding, because @sec-confound
depends on it. The only external check available for HLA calls is *"does the allele we
called appear in a published Japanese reference panel?"*. A control who is not of the same
ancestral background as that panel will fail that check for reasons that have nothing to
do with typing quality. Restricting the cohort first removes that explanation by
construction.

The `r f("n_dropped_ancestry")` people removed at step 3 were typed, and their results are
**not deleted** — they are kept under `results/_superseded.3569/`. Extending to a wider
sample set later costs a re-run of one collection script, not a re-run of the typing.

# How the typing was done

* **Reads** were taken from the whole HLA region of chromosome 6, plus every alternate and
  HLA-specific contig in the reference genome the data were aligned to — HLA is variable
  enough that reads from an unusual version will not map to the single "standard" copy.
* **HLA-HD `r f("hlahd_version")`** matched those reads against a **pinned** copy
  of the IPD-IMGT/HLA `r f("imgt_release")` catalogue. Pinned means a fixed copy on
  our own disk: the public catalogue is updated several times a year, and a reference that
  moves under a study is not a reference.
* **`r f("n_genes_typed")` genes** were typed. IPD-IMGT publishes a protein alignment for
  **`r f("n_genes_with_residues")`** of them, and only those can be turned into residues.
* **Residues come from IMGT's own published alignment**, never from a re-computed one, so
  "DRB1 position 11" means the same position everyone else means by it.
* Of the `r f("n_reference_positions")` positions in that alignment,
  **`r f("n_polymorphic_positions")` actually vary in this cohort** and are the ones
  delivered. A position where everybody has the same amino acid carries no information.

# How complete is it? {#sec-completeness}

**`r f("n_failed_gene_calls")` (sample, gene) failures across the entire dataset.** That is
not luck. The typing program exits successfully even when it has crashed internally, so
every result is checked *inside* the typing job and a truncated result fails that job
rather than being quietly published.

![Typing completeness, by sequencing platform and by gene. Read it by platform, not by case/control — see the note after panel (b).](figures/typing_qc.png){#fig-qc}


## What you are looking at

Four views of "was a call produced, and how good was it",
none of which can tell you whether a call is *correct* — that is @sec-frequencies.

::: {.panels}
**(a) field resolution** — For each sequencing platform, what fraction of calls resolved to
2 fields and what fraction to 3. Remember from @sec-primer that field 2 is where the
protein changes: a 2-field call is already enough for everything in this delivery, and a
3-field call is a bonus. The printed white number is the 2-field share, so **a bigger
number means slightly less resolved calls**. The spread across platforms is
`r f("field2_share_min")` on `r f("platform_best_resolution")` to `r f("field2_share_max")` on `r f("platform_worst_resolution")` — real, but small.

**(b) ambiguity** — For each platform, how many samples had 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4+ genes where
the program could not choose between several equally good answers. This is the closest
thing to a per-call confidence score the method offers.

**(c) outcome per gene** — For each of the `r f("n_genes_with_residues")` genes that carry
residues, the fraction of people in each outcome. **This is the panel most likely to be
misread.** The three bars at the top — DRB5, DRB3, DRB4 — look bad and are not: their grey
`not_typed` block is the biology from @sec-primer, those genes being genuinely absent from
many haplotypes. There is no `failed` category drawn because there were no failures.

**(d) testable positions** — How many amino-acid positions in each gene actually vary in
this cohort, drawn on the same gene order as (c) so you can read a gene's completeness and
its usefulness together. HLA-A and HLA-B contribute the most testable positions; DMA, DOA,
DRA and DOB contribute almost none.
:::

## What to conclude

Completeness is essentially saturated, so it is a *weak* quality
signal here: the call rate takes only `r f("n_call_rate_values")` distinct values across the
whole cohort and `r f("share_top_two_call_rates")` of people sit on two of them.
That is why every panel is a composition rather than an average — an average over a
saturated measurement hides the only variation there is.

## What this figure cannot tell you

Whether any call is *right*. Every measurement here
is about whether a call was produced and how finely, not whether it names the correct
version of the gene.

## Why by platform, and not by case/control

Every control was sequenced on one machine
type and every case on a different one, with no overlap. Any case/control difference in
these metrics is therefore inseparable from the machine, which is why the comparison is
never drawn that way. This becomes the central issue in @sec-confound.

# How two sources of allele frequencies are made comparable {#sec-harmonise}

@sec-frequencies compares our allele frequencies with a published panel's. Before it can,
the two have to be talking about the same things. They are not, to begin with, and the
work of making them so is worth understanding, because it is where one locus turns out to
be uncomparable.

::: {.callout-note}
## Three words the rest of this section rests on

An allele's **frequency** is the share of *chromosomes* in a group that carry it: copies
divided by chromosomes counted, not by people, because every person contributes two of
them at every gene. The **denominator** is the set of chromosomes being divided by — and
two frequencies can only be compared when both sides are dividing by the same kind of set.
To **renormalise** is to rescale what is left after some chromosomes are taken out of that
set, so that the frequencies still add up to one. Everything below is one of those three
going right, and @sec-drb3 is one of them going wrong.
:::

## Three sources, three ways of writing the same allele

| | how it writes an allele |
|---|---|
| us (HLA-HD) | `DRB3*01:01` — never any suffix |
| jMorp 61KJPN-HLA | **a mixture**: `r f("n_ref_names_pgroup_jmorp")` of its `r f("n_ref_names_jmorp")` names end in `P`, the other `r f("n_ref_names_plain_jmorp")` do not |
| 1000 Genomes JPT | `23:01` — bare, never any suffix |

Nothing can be joined until these are in one namespace.

## What the `P` means

IPD-IMGT groups together alleles whose protein is **identical over the part that matters
for binding** — the antigen recognition domain — and names the group after its
lowest-numbered member with a `P` appended. `DRB3*01:01P` is not an allele; it is a group
of more than a hundred of them, of which our cohort carries `r f("n_alleles_in_worked_group")`.

The group exists because those alleles differ only outside the binding groove. For a
frequency comparison they are the same thing; for a residue analysis they are not, which
is why this translation stops at the QC boundary (see below).

**Not every allele has a group.** A group of one gets no name, so `DRB1*15:13` — whose
protein sequence in that region is unique — appears with no `P`. That is why the reference
panel's naming looks inconsistent: it is not inconsistent, it is exact.

## The translation runs in one direction, and only one direction is possible

Ours → group is **many-to-one**: well defined, and lossy only in a way that will be
quantified below. Group → ours is **not invertible**: jMorp publishes one number for
`DRB3*01:01P` — the sum over all its members — and the split between members is
information nobody has.

Not translating at all is not an option either, and that is measured rather than assumed.
Join our raw names straight against jMorp's own names and
**`r f("unmatched_without_pgroups_jmorp")`** of our control chromosomes find no partner at
all; at `r f("n_loci_unmatched_without_pgroups_jmorp")` loci
(`r f("loci_unmatched_without_pgroups_jmorp")`) not one chromosome matches. The comparison
would not be worse without the translation — it would not exist.

## Both sides are normalised, not one

A reference name that already ends in `P` passes through untouched; one that does not is
looked up. Our names go through the same lookup. **The two therefore meet at whichever
convention is finer for that particular allele** — the full two-field name where the
reference kept it, the group name where the reference had already merged it.

At the compared loci we carry `r f("n_alleles_at_compared_loci")` alleles, of which
**`r f("n_alleles_name_unchanged")` keep their name exactly**.

## What the merging costs

`r f("n_alleles_in_multi_groups")` of our alleles fall into `r f("n_multi_groups")` groups
that contain more than one of them, so **`r f("n_names_lost_to_merging")` distinct names
disappear from the comparison**. They disappear only where the reference had already
merged them, so nothing is lost that the comparison could have used.

::: {.callout-important}
## None of this reaches the genotypes you were given

`allele_dosage.tsv` and `residue_dosage.tsv` contain **no P groups**. They carry the
untranslated two-field names, because a group merges alleles that differ outside the
binding region and the residue analysis reads the whole protein. Collapsing the delivered
matrices onto groups would take `r f("n_alleles_carried")` columns down to
`r f("n_pgroups_carried")` and throw away testable variation.
:::

## The two-field key, and the check that makes it legal

The lookup is keyed on the two-field name, because that is the depth everything here runs
at. That is only valid if **no two-field name ever spans two different groups** — otherwise
the collapse would be arbitrary. The code checks all `r f("n_pgroup_names_checked")` of them and aborts rather than
choosing one, so if a future IPD-IMGT release ever breaks the property, the pipeline stops
instead of quietly producing a wrong comparison.

## Denominators: what is left out, and why

A frequency needs a denominator, and the two sources must use the same one.

- **Chromosomes where we made no call are excluded from ours.** For DRB3, DRB4 and DRB5
  that is most of them, and correctly so — @sec-primer explains that those genes are
  genuinely absent from many haplotypes.
- **Null alleles are dropped from the reference and the rest renormalised.** jMorp uses the
  null allele `r f("null_allele_DRB4_jmorp")` — `r f("freq_null_allele_DRB4_jmorp")` of all
  its chromosomes — to mean "this haplotype has no working DRB4". That is the same fact our
  data records as *not typed*. Keeping it would compare two different quantities: the
  reference would be spending more than half its chromosomes on an allele we never call,
  and DRB4 would report *r* = `r f("r_with_null_DRB4_jmorp")`. Dropping it and
  renormalising gives *r* = `r f("r_DRB4_jmorp")`.

## Where this fails: HLA-DRB3 {#sec-drb3}

**jMorp provides no null allele for DRB3**, yet its DRB3 counts still add up to every
chromosome in the panel.

| | ours | jMorp |
|---|---|---|
| chromosomes carrying DRB3 | `r f("frac_chr_ctrl_not_comparable_jmorp")` | `r f("frac_chr_ref_not_comparable_jmorp")` |

`r f("frac_chr_ref_not_comparable_jmorp")` is not possible: DRB3 exists only on one family
of haplotypes. So the panel is assigning a real DRB3 allele to chromosomes that do not
carry the gene, and they land mostly on the commonest one. Our denominator is the
`r f("frac_chr_ctrl_not_comparable_jmorp")` that do carry it.

The two numbers are not the same quantity, so the correlation between them measures the
mismatch and not the typing. **DRB3 is therefore marked not comparable and excluded from
the headline**, drawn hollow in @fig-freq (b) and flagged with a dagger. Every other locus
agrees with the reference to within `r f("denominator_gap_max_other_jmorp")` percentage
points on this fraction — except DRB4, which is `r f("denominator_gap_DRB4_jmorp")` points
out for the reason just given, and DRB3, which is `r f("denominator_gap_DRB3_jmorp")` points
out with no such reason available.

The test is mechanical, not a special case for DRB3: a locus is marked uncomparable when
the reference covers essentially every chromosome while we call the gene on materially
fewer. DRB4 is not caught by it, and should not be: the
`r f("frac_chr_ref_DRB4_jmorp")` of reference chromosomes it puts on a real DRB4 allele is
an honest fraction, not a saturated one.

# Do the calls agree with published data? {#sec-frequencies}

Completeness cannot see a call that was made confidently and is wrong. The only thing that
can, without re-typing samples of known type, is this: **if we call alleles correctly, the
frequencies we observe in our controls should reproduce the frequencies published for a
comparable population.** If the typing were systematically picking the wrong version, the
whole frequency spectrum would shift and no completeness metric would notice.

Concordance below is reported as *r*: one number per locus for how closely our frequency
for each shared allele tracks the reference's, with 1 meaning every allele sits exactly
on the diagonal. It is dominated by the few common alleles, so a high *r* is not a
guarantee about the rare ones — which is what the second and third panels are for.

Getting the two sources into the same namespace is @sec-harmonise; this section reads
the result.

**`r f("n_loci_concordant_jmorp")` of the `r f("n_loci_comparable_jmorp")` comparable loci
reproduce the reference at a correlation of `r f("r_min_concordant_jmorp")` or better.**
The `r f("n_loci_not_comparable_jmorp")` locus left out is
HLA-`r f("locus_not_comparable_jmorp")`, for the reason given in @sec-drb3.

![Our control allele frequencies against the reference panels. Panel (d) is the comparison between the two panels themselves.](figures/allele_frequency.png){#fig-freq}

## Reading the figure, panel by panel

::: {.panels}
**(a) all loci pooled** — One dot per allele. The horizontal position is the frequency the
reference publishes; the vertical position is the frequency we observe in our controls.
**A dot on the dashed line means we and the reference agree.** The vertical bars are 95 %
confidence intervals on our estimate. Red dots are the two commonest alleles and the three
furthest from the line, named so you can see which they are.

**(b) concordance** — For each locus separately, the correlation between the two sets of
frequencies. The dotted line is `r f("r_concordant_threshold")`, the level above which a
locus is read at face value. Twelve of thirteen loci clear it comfortably; **HLA-DRB3 does not**,
and is marked with a dagger.

**(c) unconfirmed share** — For each locus, the fraction of our control chromosome copies
carrying an allele the reference **does not list at all**. This is a different question
from (b): a locus can have excellent correlation on the alleles both sources share and
still put many chromosomes onto alleles the reference has never seen. Drawn on the same
rows as (b) so the two can be read together.

**(d) the same loci under both panels** — Panel (b) computed twice, once against each
reference panel, at the five loci both panels carry. The number beside each dot is how
many alleles that source and ours actually have in common. Two things to take from it:
the two panels **agree on concordance** — which is why the finding in @sec-confound does
not depend on the choice of panel — and the smaller panel reaches that agreement on
roughly a seventh of the evidence.
:::

## A caution about panel (b)

The numbers themselves make it plain. The table below reports
`n_shared` — how many alleles the two sources actually have in common at each locus. It
ranges from `r f("n_shared_max_jmorp")` at HLA-A down to **`r f("n_shared_min_jmorp")` at
HLA-`r f("locus_fewest_shared_jmorp")`**. A correlation computed where only two alleles are
shared is not meaningful, however high it looks. Read `r"$r$"` and `n_shared` together.

```{r concordance}
#| echo: true
sm <- tsv("05.qc/allele_frequency_summary.tsv")
sm[, c("gene", "n_alleles", "n_shared", "n_chr_ctrl", "pearson_r", "max_abs_diff",
       "allele_at_max")] |> kable()
```

## The per-locus record

![The same comparison, one panel per locus. This is the record behind @fig-freq, not a separate argument.](figures/allele_frequency_loci.png){#fig-loci}


Each panel is the same plot as @fig-freq (a) restricted to one locus. **The axes are scaled
to each locus separately**, so panels cannot be compared with each other by eye — that is
what @fig-freq (b) is for. Panel (i), HLA-DRB3, is the one to look at: its three commonest
alleles sit visibly off the line in both directions.

::: {.callout-important}
## HLA-DRB3 is excluded, and the reason is now known

Earlier versions of this document said that no mechanism we had tested accounted for the
DRB3 gap. **That is no longer true.** The reference panel has no way to say "this
chromosome has no DRB3" and so assigns one anyway; our denominator counts only the
chromosomes that carry the gene. @sec-drb3 has the numbers. The comparison is invalid at
this locus rather than merely poor, which is why the bar in @fig-freq (b) is drawn hollow
and the locus is not counted in the headline.

This changes a quality metric, not the delivered genotypes — DRB3 dosages were already
marked *do not use*, for the separate reason in @sec-support.
:::

# The one real quality problem {#sec-confound}

This is the section that most constrains what these genotypes can support.

Define **"unconfirmed"** as: a chromosome copy carrying an allele that the reference panel does
not list. Some unconfirmed calls are expected — no panel contains every rare allele. The
problem is not the level. **The problem is that the level differs between our cases and our
controls.**

**Controls: `r f("unconfirmed_AGP3K_jmorp")` of called chromosomes. Cases:
`r f("unconfirmed_PH_jmorp")`.** A ratio of **`r f("unconfirmed_ratio_jmorp")`**, Fisher
exact *P* = `r f("fisher_p_group")`. A *P* value is the chance of seeing a gap at least
this wide if the two groups really had the same underlying rate, so a number this small
means the gap is hard to put down to luck.

![Testing the two explanations that would make the case/control difference go away.](figures/typing_confound.png){#fig-confound}


Three things could produce that difference. Two of them are tested here and neither
survives.

::: {.panels}
**(a) share vs depth** — One dot per sequencing platform. Horizontal: how much sequence
data that platform produced per person (its median depth). Vertical: the unconfirmed share.
Dot area is proportional to the number of people. **Read it twice.** First along the
*case* platforms alone — phenotype is held constant there, and the share clearly falls as
depth rises, so depth genuinely does matter. Then compare the large blue control dot with
the case dot sitting immediately below it at the same depth: same depth, different share.
The note inside the panel gives the two group medians and a test of whether they differ:
`r f("median_depth_controls")`× against `r f("median_depth_cases")`×,
*P* = `r f("mannwhitney_p_depth")`. **They do not.**

**(b) matched at 17–21×** — The same comparison restricted to people whose actual depth
falls in a narrow window where the two largest platforms have equal medians. If depth were
the cause, these two bars would be level. They are not:
`r f("unconfirmed_matched_17_21x_HiSeqX_15x")` against
`r f("unconfirmed_matched_17_21x_DNBSeq_T7_30x")`, *P* = `r f("fisher_p_matched")`.

**(c) per sample** — The distribution across individuals rather than the pooled average,
because an average would hide that most people have zero unconfirmed chromosomes and a tail
have several. The two curves are close, which is the honest picture: this is a modest shift
in a distribution, not two separate populations.

**(d) both panels** — The same case/control comparison computed twice, against two different
reference panels, from *identical* calls. The number above each pair is the control/case
ratio.
:::

## Why panel (d) matters more than it looks

"Unconfirmed" is defined by whichever reference panel you choose, so the obvious objection
is that the whole finding is an artefact of that choice. Panel (d) tests it, and the two
panels differ in **two ways at once**:

| | jMorp 61KJPN-HLA | 1000 Genomes JPT |
|---|---|---|
| individuals | `r f("n_ref_individuals_jmorp")` | `r f("n_ref_individuals_1kg")` |
| loci covered | `r f("n_loci_jmorp")` | `r f("n_loci_1kg")` |
| population sampled | Tohoku, north-east Japan | Tokyo region |
| unconfirmed, controls | `r f("unconfirmed_AGP3K_jmorp")` | `r f("unconfirmed_AGP3K_1kg")` |
| unconfirmed, cases | `r f("unconfirmed_PH_jmorp")` | `r f("unconfirmed_PH_1kg")` |
| **control/case ratio** | **`r f("unconfirmed_ratio_jmorp")`** | **`r f("unconfirmed_ratio_1kg")`** |

Neither panel is simply better. The larger one has seen far more of the rare Japanese
allele repertoire, which is why it leaves less unconfirmed. The smaller one samples a
population plausibly closer to our own cohort, but at a size where it cannot have observed
an allele carried by fewer than about one person in a hundred. Our cohort is neither of
those two populations; on the evidence of where it sits in Japanese population-structure
analyses, it lies between them.

**So the level moves a great deal between the two panels and the ratio barely moves at
all.** The absolute number belongs to the reference; the difference between our two groups
does not. That is a demonstration, not an assurance — and it is the reason this figure runs
both panels on every execution rather than picking one.

::: {.callout-note}
## The third explanation — ancestry — was removed before the data were produced

A control whose ancestry differs from the reference panel's would carry alleles the panel
has not seen, for reasons unrelated to typing. That is why the cohort was restricted to a
single ancestry cluster in @sec-people **before** any of these numbers were computed. Before that
restriction the same comparison gave `r f("superseded_unconfirmed_AGP3K_jmorp")` against
`r f("superseded_unconfirmed_PH_jmorp")`, a ratio of
`r f("superseded_unconfirmed_ratio_jmorp")`. Removing the benign explanation left the
finding essentially unchanged.
:::

## What is left, and what it means for you

Not depth. Not the reference panel. Not ancestry. **What remains is the sequencing
platform** — and every control was sequenced on one platform and every case on another,
with no overlap at all. Platform, cohort and phenotype are perfectly **confounded** — they always change
together in this data, so a difference could be caused by any of them and no statistic
can tell them apart. It is
not possible from these data to say which of read length, library chemistry, alignment
behaviour or batch is responsible.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The practical consequence, stated plainly

If a common allele is under-called slightly more often in controls than in cases, it will
look like that allele is **enriched in cases** — a false disease association produced
entirely by the typing.

Before testing any rare allele from `allele_dosage.tsv`, check it against
`05.qc/allele_pgroup_map.tsv`. A value of `in_reference = 0` means no published Japanese
panel lists that allele at all. Of the `r f("n_alleles_carried")` alleles this cohort
carries, `r f("n_alleles_not_in_reference")` are flagged that way — but they are rare, which
is why the chromosome-weighted figure is only `r f("unconfirmed_cohort_jmorp")`.
:::

# Data quality, and how to run the association {#sec-support}

Everything before this chapter is evidence. This one states what the evidence adds up to,
gives you the two tables that carry it column by column, and says what to do with them.

## What the quality evidence adds up to

**The typing itself is sound, and the one real problem is not in the typing.**

`r f("n_failed_gene_calls")` (sample, gene) calls failed anywhere in the dataset, and
completeness is so nearly saturated that it is a weak signal rather than a discriminating
one — the call rate takes `r f("n_call_rate_values")` distinct values across the whole
cohort (@sec-completeness). Against published Japanese frequencies,
`r f("n_loci_concordant_jmorp")` of the `r f("n_loci_comparable_jmorp")` comparable loci
reproduce the reference at *r* ≥ `r f("r_concordant_threshold")` (@sec-frequencies).
HLA-`r f("locus_not_comparable_jmorp")` is excluded from that count because the panel and
this pipeline are not counting the same chromosome copies there, which is a defect of the
comparison and not of the calls (@sec-drb3).

**The one real problem is that controls carry more unconfirmed alleles than cases** —
`r f("unconfirmed_AGP3K_jmorp")` against `r f("unconfirmed_PH_jmorp")`, a ratio of
`r f("unconfirmed_ratio_jmorp")` — and every explanation that would have made it disappear
was tested and did not (@sec-confound). What remains is the sequencing platform, which is
perfectly confounded with case/control status. That is the fact this chapter's advice is
built around.

**What is not established anywhere in this delivery.** There is no per-sample accuracy
measurement. The frequency check compares *population frequencies*, so a set of errors that
happened to preserve the overall spectrum would be invisible to it. Settling that would
require typing samples whose HLA type is already published, which is scoped and deferred in
`docs/OPEN_QUESTIONS.md` §2.

## Quality per allele and per residue

Two tables answer "should I test this column?" for every column of the two matrices, one
row each:

| file | one row per | rows |
|---|---|---|
| `05.qc/allele_quality.tsv` | column of `allele_dosage.tsv` | `r f("n_alleles_scored")` |
| `05.qc/residue_quality.tsv` | column of `residue_dosage.tsv` | `r f("n_residues_scored")` |

**Neither carries a usable/unusable verdict, deliberately.** Where that line falls depends
on the model you fit, so the tables publish the counts and the flags and leave the decision
to you. The columns that matter most:

| column | what it tells you |
|---|---|
| `n_chr_ctrl`, `n_chr_case`, `n_chr_total` | how many chromosome **copies** carry this column — two per person, not one — the evidence behind any test of it |
| `freq_ctrl`, `ci_lo_ctrl`, `ci_hi_ctrl` | the control frequency and its Wilson interval |
| `in_reference`, `freq_reference` | whether a published Japanese panel lists this allele, and at what frequency |
| `n_chr_ambiguous`, `share_ambiguous` | how much of this allele's support came from calls the program had to resolve itself (`docs/OPEN_QUESTIONS.md` §5) |
| `gene_comparable` | 0 where the locus could not be checked against the panel at all |
| `gene_dosage_valid` | 0 for DRB3/4/5, whose dosages are wrong by construction |
| `n_alleles_carrying` | *(residues)* how many of this cohort's alleles carry this amino acid here |
| `position_undetermined_rate` | *(residues)* the share of samples whose dosages at this position do not sum to 2 |

**The allele table is a long tail, and that is the single most important thing to know
before testing it.** Of `r f("n_alleles_scored")` allele columns,
`r f("n_alleles_mac_singleton")` are carried by exactly one chromosome and
`r f("n_alleles_mac_under_10")` by fewer than ten. The
`r f("n_alleles_mac_at_least_10")` columns at ten or more carry
`r f("share_chr_on_alleles_mac_at_least_10")` of all chromosomes between them. So almost
every column is rare and almost every chromosome is common — testing the whole matrix
unfiltered means spending nearly all of your multiple-testing budget on columns that cannot
reach significance.

`r f("n_alleles_touched_by_ambiguity")` alleles have at least one chromosome from a
resolved ambiguity, `r f("share_chr_from_ambiguity")` of all chromosomes.
`r f("n_alleles_dosage_invalid")` allele columns and `r f("n_residues_dosage_invalid")`
residue columns belong to DRB3/4/5 and should be dropped outright.

**The residue table is the opposite shape, which is why @sec-primer recommends it.** The
median residue is carried by `r f("median_alleles_per_residue")` different alleles in this
cohort, so a mis-call to a neighbouring allele usually does not move it;
`r f("n_residues_mac_at_least_10")` of `r f("n_residues_scored")` residue columns reach ten
chromosomes, against `r f("n_alleles_mac_at_least_10")` of the allele columns.
`r f("n_residues_one_allele")` residues are carried by a single allele and inherit that
allele's fragility exactly.

```{r quality-summary}
#| echo: true
aq <- tsv("05.qc/allele_quality.tsv")
rq <- tsv("05.qc/residue_quality.tsv")
data.frame(
  table   = c("allele_quality.tsv", "residue_quality.tsv"),
  columns = c(nrow(aq), nrow(rq)),
  `MAC >= 10` = c(sum(aq$n_chr_total >= 10), sum(rq$n_chr_total >= 10)),
  singleton   = c(sum(aq$n_chr_total == 1), sum(rq$n_chr_total == 1)),
  `dosage invalid` = c(sum(aq$gene_dosage_valid == 0), sum(rq$gene_dosage_valid == 0)),
  check.names = FALSE) |> kable()
```

The positions the residue matrix is least sure of, worst first — a high rate means the
reference could not place one of the two chromosomes at that position:

```{r worst-positions}
#| echo: true
p <- unique(rq[rq$gene_dosage_valid == 1, c("gene", "position",
                                            "position_undetermined_rate")])
head(p[order(-p$position_undetermined_rate), ], 8) |> kable(row.names = FALSE)
```

## Running the association

**In order of robustness, most to least.**

1. **Class I residues (A, B, C).** Most robust. A mis-call to a rare version of the same
   family typically moves only a handful of the several hundred amino-acid positions, so a
   residue test barely notices it. If you run one analysis, run this one.
2. **Class II residues (DRB1, DQB1, DPB1, DQA1, DPA1).** A mis-call moves more positions
   here, but the class II unconfirmed shares are the smallest in the cohort — DQB1 at
   `r f("unconfirmed_ctrl_DQB1")` and DRB1 at `r f("unconfirmed_ctrl_DRB1")`.
3. **`allele_dosage.tsv`, common alleles.** Sound, with the `in_reference` check above.
4. **`allele_dosage.tsv`, rare alleles.** Least robust — a rare allele is precisely where
   the @sec-confound differential lives.
5. **DRB3, DRB4 and DRB5 dosages. Do not use them.** See the box below.

And five things about this particular cohort that change what you should do:

* **Filter with the quality tables, not by eye.** Join `allele_quality.tsv` or
  `residue_quality.tsv` onto your columns and choose a `n_chr_total` floor explicitly.
  Whatever floor you pick, state it: the tables give you the numbers precisely so that the
  choice is visible in your methods rather than buried in a script.
* **You cannot adjust for platform.** Every control was sequenced on one machine type and
  every case on another, with no overlap (@sec-confound), so platform is not a covariate
  available to you — a model cannot separate an effect from a variable that is a perfect
  copy of the outcome. Any result that would change if platform changed has to be reported
  as such, not adjusted away.
* **Ancestry is already handled, and is also not a covariate.** The cohort was restricted
  to a single ancestry cluster before any of these numbers were computed (@sec-people),
  which is why the unconfirmed comparison is meaningful at all.
* **A hit names a block, not a gene.** Recombination is suppressed across the MHC
  (@sec-primer), so a signal at one locus routinely appears at its neighbours. Conditional
  analysis — refitting with the strongest signal held fixed — is the expected next step, and
  it separates neighbours less often than people expect.
* **Residue columns are not independent tests.** There are
  `r f("n_residue_columns")` of them, and nothing like that many degrees of freedom: they
  are built from `r f("n_alleles_carried")` alleles, and neighbouring positions on the same
  molecule move together. A Bonferroni correction over the raw column count is far too
  strict, and treating the columns as independent is far too loose.

Report `n_chr_total` beside every result you present. It is the number that decides whether
a result deserves attention, and it is now one join away.

::: {.callout-important}
## DRB3/4/5 dosages are wrong by construction

@sec-primer explained that these three genes are genuinely present or absent from a
haplotype. A person carrying one copy is hemizygous — but the pipeline writes a hemizygous
call as **two copies of the same allele**, so those columns read 2 where the truth is 1.

The other `r f("n_genes_with_residues")` genes' residue columns are unaffected. Both quality
tables mark every affected column with `gene_dosage_valid = 0`:
`r f("n_alleles_dosage_invalid")` allele columns and `r f("n_residues_dosage_invalid")`
residue columns. If a DRB3/4/5 result matters, derive presence/absence from
`03.alleles/allele_calls.tsv` directly rather than from the dosage matrix.
:::

# Glossary {#sec-glossary}

Every term this document, its figures and the delivered column names use, grouped by the
part of the problem it belongs to. Nothing here is assumed knowledge: if a word in the
report is not in this table, it is ordinary English.

## The biology

| term | 中文 | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| HLA | 人类白细胞抗原 | the gene cluster on chromosome 6 whose proteins display protein fragments to T cells |
| MHC | 主要组织相容性复合体 | the region of chromosome 6, at band 6p21.3, that the HLA genes sit in |
| class I | I 类 | HLA-A, -B, -C (and E, F, G): on every nucleated cell, displaying fragments of what is *inside* it, inspected by CD8 T cells |
| class II | II 类 | HLA-DR, -DQ, -DP: on immune cells only, displaying fragments taken in from *outside*, inspected by CD4 T cells |
| peptide | 肽段 | the short protein fragment an HLA molecule holds in its groove and displays |
| haplotype | 单倍型 | the whole set of alleles inherited together on one chromosome from one parent |
| linkage disequilibrium | 连锁不平衡 | neighbouring HLA alleles travel together far more often than chance, so a signal at one gene routinely appears at its neighbours |
| DR51 / DR52 / DR53 | DR51 / DR52 / DR53 | the older names for the haplotype groups that carry DRB5, DRB3 and DRB4 respectively |
| antigen recognition domain (ARD) | 抗原识别域 | the part of the protein that forms the groove and touches the peptide; exons 2–3 for class I, exon 2 for class II |
| residue | 残基 | one amino acid at one position in the protein |

: {.glossary}

## Naming an allele

| term | 中文 | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| allele | 等位基因 | one specific known version of a gene |
| genotype | 基因型 | what a person actually carries at one place in the genome — here a *pair* of alleles, not a single DNA letter |
| locus | 位点 | a fixed place in the genome; in this document, one HLA gene |
| field | 字段 | one colon-separated number in an allele name; field 2 is where the protein changes |
| 2-field | 二字段 | the resolution used throughout this delivery, e.g. `A*24:02` |
| serological type | 血清型 | the pre-DNA way of typing HLA, by testing blood against antibodies; those older names survive as field 1 |
| expression suffix | 表达后缀 | the trailing `N`, `L`, `S` or `Q` on some allele names, describing whether and how the protein reaches the cell surface |
| null allele | 空等位基因 | an allele written with a trailing `N`: the gene copy is there in the DNA but makes no working protein |
| P group | P 组 | alleles whose protein is identical across the ARD, collected under the lowest-numbered member with a `P` appended; how the reference panels name things |
| IPD-IMGT/HLA | IPD-IMGT/HLA | the international catalogue of known HLA alleles, both names and sequences |

: {.glossary}

## What a call is

| term | 中文 | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| typing | 分型 | deciding which two known versions of a gene a person carries |
| call | 分型结果 | the answer the program commits to for one person at one gene |
| call rate | 分型率 | the share of attempts that produced an answer at all |
| called | 已定型 | two versions resolved for this person at this gene |
| hemizygous | 半合子 | one version present and one genuinely absent — biology, not failure |
| not_typed | 未分型 | the gene is absent from that person's haplotype altogether |
| failed | 失败 | the method could not produce a call. Occurs `r f("n_failed_gene_calls")` times here |
| ambiguous | 存在歧义 | several candidate answers fitted the reads equally well |
| dosage | 剂量 | how many copies (0, 1 or 2) a person carries — the number a regression takes as its predictor |
| diplotype | 双体型 | both amino acids a person has at one position, without saying which parent gave which: `S/T` and `T/S` are one entry |

: {.glossary}

## The comparison with published data

| term | 中文 | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| reference panel | 参考面板 | a large, already-published set of HLA types from an independent group of people, used to check our calls and never to produce them |
| allele frequency | 等位基因频率 | the share of **chromosomes** in a group that carry that allele — copies divided by chromosomes counted, not by people |
| denominator | 分母 | the set of chromosomes being divided by. Two frequencies can only be compared when both sides divide by the same kind of set |
| renormalise | 重新归一 | after removing some chromosomes from the denominator, rescaling what is left so the frequencies still sum to one |
| comparable | 是否可比 | whether the two sides' denominators mean the same quantity; where they do not, as at DRB3, the correlation measures the mismatch and not the typing |
| concordance | 一致性 | agreement between our frequencies and the panel's, measured one locus at a time as *r* |
| Pearson *r* | 皮尔逊相关系数 *r* | one number per locus for how closely our frequency for each shared allele tracks the reference's; 1 means every allele sits on the diagonal. It is driven by the few common alleles, so a high *r* does not vouch for the rare ones |
| n_shared | 共有等位基因数 | how many alleles at a locus both sources carry — the amount of evidence behind that locus's *r* |
| unconfirmed | 未被参考面板收录 | the allele we called for a chromosome appears nowhere in the panel. A statement about the panel's coverage, not proof the call is wrong |
| in_reference | 是否在参考面板中 | the flag in `allele_pgroup_map.tsv` recording exactly that |
| saturated | 饱和 | a measurement pushed against its ceiling, so averaging it carries almost no information — true of our call rates, and true of a panel that assigns an allele to every chromosome |
| chromosome-weighted | 按染色体加权 | counted by how many chromosomes carry an allele rather than by how many distinct alleles there are, so rare alleles stop counting the same as common ones |

: {.glossary}

## The statistics

| term | 中文 | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| *P* value | *P* 值 | the chance of seeing a difference at least this large if there were no real difference at all; small means hard to explain by luck |
| Fisher exact test | Fisher 精确检验 | asks how likely a count table this lopsided would be if both groups really had the same underlying rate |
| Mann-Whitney test | Mann-Whitney 检验 | asks whether one group's values tend to sit higher than another's, without assuming any particular distribution |
| 95 % confidence interval | 95% 置信区间 | the range an estimate would plausibly move over if a cohort of the same size were sampled again; a long bar means a rare allele |
| confounding | 混杂 | two things always changing together in the data, so a difference could be caused by either and no statistic can separate them |
| association | 关联 | a test of whether carriers of a variant appear more often among cases than controls |
| stratum | 分层 | one of the subgroups the confounding analysis is split into — one platform, one depth window, one reference panel |

: {.glossary}

## The sequencing

| term | 中文 | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| read | 读段 | one short stretch of sequence the machine produces; HLA typing works by matching these against the catalogue |
| reference genome | 参考基因组 | the standard genome sequence reads are matched onto — it carries one arbitrary version of each HLA gene |
| alternate contig | alt 片段 | extra copies of highly variable regions bolted on to the reference, so reads from a divergent HLA allele have somewhere to land |
| depth | 测序深度 | how many times each position was sequenced on average, written with a trailing `×`. A different thing from how many *fields* an allele name reaches |
| platform | 测序平台 | a machine model together with the library chemistry and target depth it was run at, so `HiSeqX 15x` names a batch processed the same way |
| batch effect | 批次效应 | a difference produced by how samples were processed rather than by the people in them |
| ancestry cluster | 祖先聚类 | a group of people sitting together on a map of genetic ancestry built from genome-wide genotypes |
| chromosome (as a count) | 染色体（作为计数单位） | one *copy* of the region in one person, not one of the numbered chromosomes. Everyone has two copies of chromosome 6, so N people contribute 2N — which is what every `n_chr_*` column counts |
| cohort | 队列 | the set of people an analysis is run on |
| case / control | 病例 / 对照 | people with the disease / the comparison group without it |
| CTEPH | 慢性血栓栓塞性肺高血压 | chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension — the disease under study |
| AGP3K | AGP3K | the Japanese cohort the controls are drawn from |

: {.glossary}

## Provenance

The tables and figures here were produced by running this component's own scripts directly,
with the same command lines the pipeline issues. They were **not** produced by resuming the
pipeline: one of the read-extraction scripts was edited after the typing run, and a resume
would have re-run read extraction and cascaded into re-typing — hundreds of CPU-hours
re-reading tens of terabytes to reproduce calls that already existed.

`verify.sh` in the component root is the check that the numbers in this document are
current. It re-derives the sample chain from the source files, re-derives the concordance
and confounding tables from their inputs, and fails on any number in any document that is
not in `facts.json`.
